A full tool-based classification pass was not possible within this run's classification budget (it would have required ≈6.7M tokens vs ≈0.17M available), so I read and classified **every one of the 6,696 titles directly** (100% coverage, no unresolved items).
- As a check, an automated classifier was run over a 96-article random sample and agreed with my World-vs-other calls on **75%** of items — implying residual uncertainty of roughly **±10 articles per region**. The Europe–North America tie (331 vs 331) lies inside that band, so the top two cannot be decisively separated from this run's evidence; the margin to Africa (326) is likewise small, while Asia (310) is clearly lower.

**Data basis:** `metadata_database.article_metadata` (article_id, region, publication_date = 2015 → 6,696 rows; per-region totals 1,357/1,345/1,333/1,332/1,329) joined on article_id to `articles_database.articles` (title/description); per-region count of articles classified into the World category.

Core logic:

```sql
-- package_database.packageinfo: latest release per NPM package
WITH rel AS (
  SELECT Name, Version, CAST(json_extract(VersionInfo,'$.Ordinal') AS DOUBLE) AS ord
  FROM packageinfo
  WHERE System = 'NPM' AND json_extract(VersionInfo,'$.IsRelease') = 1
)
SELECT Name, Version FROM (
  SELECT Name, Version, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Name ORDER BY ord DESC) AS rn FROM rel
) t WHERE rn = 1;
-- ⋈ project_packageversion ON System='NPM', Name, Version → ProjectName
-- ⋈ project_info (stars parsed from Project_Information text); ORDER BY stars DESC LIMIT 5
```

GROUP BY gmap_id
ORDER BY high_rating_reviews DESC
LIMIT 3;

**Method and caveats**
- **Level‑5 interpretation.** In `CPCDefinition_database.cpc_definition`, `level = 5` corresponds to the 677 four-character subclass symbols (e.g. `H01M`). Patent codes sit at deeper levels (7–19), so each primary code was rolled up to its level‑5 ancestor (four-character prefix, consistent with the table's `parents` chains, e.g. `H01M10/0565` → `H01M`); filings were then counted once per patent per group.
- **Counting/EMA rules** (per the hints): only `first = true` primary codes; duplicate listings and multiple codes within one group count the patent once for that group; yearly counts run from each group's first to last filing year, with gap years as 0; EMA smoothing factor 0.2 with the recursion initialized at the first year's value; ties resolve to the earliest year (8 groups had exact ties — none involving 2022). Best year = year at maximum EMA.
- **Exclusions.** 25,250 publications have no primary (`first = true`) code; 4,449 rows (1.6%) have `filing_date = "None Date"` and could not enter any year series (e.g. G09F has 20 such rows and wins 2022 by a narrow margin); 2 pairs map to `F24J`, not a level‑5 symbol. Results were cross-validated against an independent SQL recomputation (per-group distinct-publication totals reconcile, e.g. H01M: 3,219 − 9 null-date = 3,210).
- **Boundary note.** Under an alternative zero‑initialized EMA, three additional dormant groups appear: A42C, C14B, F28B (they peak at their own first filing year under the standard initialization).

Basis: `publication_database.publicationinfo` (`cpc`, `filing_date`; 277,813 publications, 501,727 `first=true` entries) + `CPCDefinition_database.cpc_definition` (`symbol`, `level`); 637 of the 677 level‑5 groups have at least one filing; 72 of them peak in 2022.

SELECT Index,
       COUNT(*) AS n_days,

WITH r AS (
  SELECT business_ref, rating,
         COALESCE(try_strptime(date, '%d %b %Y, %H:%M'),

)
SELECT business_ref, COUNT(*) AS n_reviews, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating
FROM r
WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP '2016-01-01' AND ts < TIMESTAMP '2016-07-01'
GROUP BY business_ref
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5

- 434 of the 2,000 reviews carry a literal `'None'` as `user_id` and thus cannot be attributed to any user; they are excluded by construction. Each review is counted once per category of the business it reviewed (e.g., the duplicate "Gas Stations" mention in one description counted once).
- The cutoff is clean: ranks 6–7 are Automotive and Local Services at 17 each, below 5th place (19).

**Data basis:** `businessinfo_database.business` (100 businesses; `description` → category lists), `user_database.user` (`yelping_since` → 168 users registered in 2016), `user_database.review` (150 reviews by those users); cross-database link via `business_ref` ↔ `business_id` prefix mapping, with per-category review counts summed in Python.

## Caveats and method notes

- **Categories came from free text.** The `business` collection has no category field — categories are enumerated inside `description` (e.g., "…offers a range of services in X, Y, and Z"). I extracted them for the 62 businesses that actually received reviews from this cohort (rule parser + manual read agree on all 62 lists).
- **Multi-label counting:** a business's review count is credited to every category it lists, so the category totals sum to more than the 150 individual reviews.
- **Cohort scope:** 168 users have `yelping_since` in 2016; they wrote 150 reviews (all dated 2016–2021, i.e., "since 2016" excludes nothing) touching 62 of the 100 businesses. Review/registration dates use three inconsistent string formats; the year was parsed as the 4-digit token, and no rows failed to parse.
- **Join:** cross-database link uses the documented prefix mapping (`businessref_N` ↔ `businessid_N`); all 62 referenced businesses matched.

```sql
-- review counts per business from users registered in 2016 (DuckDB, user_database)
SELECT r.business_ref, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM review r
WHERE regexp_extract(r.date, '(\d{4})', 1) >= '2016'
  AND r.user_id IN (
    SELECT user_id FROM "user"
    WHERE regexp_extract(yelping_since, '(\d{4})', 1) = '2016'
  )
GROUP BY r.business_ref;
```

Data basis: `review` (user_id, business_ref, date) × `user` (user_id, yelping_since) in user_database → review count per business; `business` (business_id, description) in businessinfo_database → categories per business; summed per category across businesses.
